result.killer: Partial, not fatal: FBR's free DNFBP mobile app (registration, proscribed-person screening, STR generation) plus FMU goAML and simplified FBR CDD forms cover the core screening and reporting steps. Weak enforcement (IMF finding) and low willingness to pay among small dealers further limit demand. Not checked: S.R.O. 1439(I)/2026 text, and whether the NOC bar on unregistered builders took effect.
result.reason: I found no Pakistani vendor that keeps the full CDD, record-retention and compliance-officer file for property dealers or builders. Global KYC/AML SaaS (Shufti Pro, AML Watcher) is built for banks and fintechs and does not target this group. However, FBR's free DNFBP app (iOS id1560978125) already handles registration, screening against the proscribed-persons list (CNIC/name) and STR generation, and FBR has simplified CDD forms. That leaves only file-keeping and risk assessment to sell. The market is real but thin: about 22,000 registered agents out of an estimated 500,000 dealers. Enforcement is weak; the IMF called DNFBP supervision unsatisfactory and STR numbers extremely low. Sole-trader dealers are unlikely to pay. Builders under S.R.O. 1439 are a better niche, but their NOC bar is unverified.

result.competitor: I found no commercial MSDS readiness software or Pakistani consultancy in English searches. I did not search in Urdu, so informal local consultants are not ruled out. Free state alternatives cover much of the core job: PHC publishes MSDS manuals by facility type for download on os.phc.org.pk, trains facility staff on MSDS, and runs the HCE web portal. SHCC launched an online registration and licensing system in June 2025, linked to the Sindh Business One Stop Shop. Third-party MSDS checklists also circulate free on Scribd.
result.duty: Healthcare establishments must register and get a licence from their provincial commission: PHC Act 2010 (Punjab), SHCC Act 2013 (Sindh), KP HCC Act 2015. Punjab: registration, then a provisional licence and the MSDS manual, then up to 6 months to comply before inspection. Full compliance gives a regular licence, partial compliance a conditional one. Fines go up to Rs500,000, or the facility is closed until it complies. PHC set a 31 Jul 2025 MSDS deadline and restarted inspections on 1 Aug 2025. It made over 18,500 inspection visits in a recent fiscal year (April APP report, year not stated) and is nearly through all allopathic facilities. Sindh: a regular licence needs more than 90% compliance and no critical issues, and is valid 5 years. A July 2026 Tribune report found 11 of 18 Karachi facilities unregistered and gave 7-day notices. Recurrence is weak: licence renewal every 5 years plus surprise inspections. There is no regular filing.
result.market: Punjab: 60,690 HCEs registered, public and private (undated PHC board figure). A 2021 figure was more than 64,000 registered and 41,000 licensed. Sindh: 11,802 registration forms, 827 in inspection, and only 86 private facilities with a regular licence (2018-2024, Dawn). KP: 23,041 registered in total, 2,574 new in 2025-26. The claim's '23,041 across KP, Sindh and Punjab' is wrong; that is KP alone. Roughly 95,000 registered across the three provinces, mostly small clinics.
result.reason: The duty is real. Under the PHC Act 2010, SHCC Act 2013 and KP HCC Act 2015, every clinic, lab and dental clinic needs a licence. A regular licence (5 years in Punjab and Sindh) is granted only after an inspection against the MSDS (Minimum Service Delivery Standards). Penalties: fines up to Rs500,000, then sealing. Enforcement rose in 2025-26. I found no commercial readiness software. The PHC gives out its MSDS manuals (about 18-23 standards and 47-74 indicators per facility type) and the staff training free. The claim's 23,041 figure is KP only, not three provinces. The checklist is small and done once every five years, and doctors resent the regime. That points to low willingness to pay and low frequency. Merge with K06.

result.duty: Punjab Provincial Motor Vehicles (Third Amendment) Ordinance 2026, promulgated by the governor in late July 2026 and in force immediately. It inserts Chapter VI-A into the Provincial Motor Vehicles Ordinance 1965 (ss.74-A/74-B). Vehicles whose registration lapsed or was cancelled under s.35, that fail fitness or emission checks under s.39-A, or that are written off must be scrapped at a private authorised or government facility. Scrapping covers depollution, dismantling, parts recovery and crushing. The duties on facilities (licensing, certificate of destruction, registers, reporting frequency, penalties) are left to rules that were not yet notified in any source found as of the latest coverage (Aug 21, 2026); no gazette notification of rules was found. No report of the Punjab Assembly passing a replacement bill was found. Ordinances usually lapse unless replaced, which would be around late Oct 2026 (not verified). The duty on the businesses themselves is therefore not yet defined: not_reached.
result.market: No register or statistic of dismantlers or scrap yards in Punjab was found. Large informal clusters exist: Bilal Gunj in Lahore (no shop count found) and Sultan Ka Khoo in Rawalpindi (reported 900+ spare-parts shops). Most are informal parts dealers, not prospective authorised facilities. The number of facilities that will seek authorisation is unknown and likely small (tens) at first.
result.reason: The law exists: the Provincial Motor Vehicles (Third Amendment) Ordinance 2026 adds Chapter VI-A on end-of-life vehicles. Agencies such as Pakistan Progressive Associates and Asil describe their own in-house pipelines. Generic ERPs (Odoo, Ramco for GCC manpower firms) exist but have no BEOE module. result.duty: Federal Emigration Ordinance 1979 and Emigration Rules 1979 (updated 2023, S.R.O. 1058(I)/2023), administered by BEOE. Per the BEOE FAQ (search snippet), a licence is valid for 3 calendar years. Renewal is on Form 3 through the Protector of Emigrants, at least 1 month before expiry, at Rs15,000 per year plus a Rs1,000 late fee. The renewal period depends on workers sent in the last 3 years: 50 or more gives 3 years, 10-49 gives 2 years, fewer than 10 gives 1 year. The Director-General can refuse renewal for misconduct, poor performance or breaches. Penalties include suspension, cancellation and loss of the security deposit. The BEOE news feed shows suspensions and show-cause notices to OEPs (e.g. Jul-Aug 2025). The per-worker demand-permission and emigrant protector registration are recurring, but they run on BEOE systems. Not reached: whether the Rules require periodic returns or registers. Both copies of the Rules failed to open (BEOE PDF returned 403; the FIA PDF could not be read).
result.market: 4,685 OEPs registered with BEOE. Of these, 2,358 held valid licences in January 2026; 1,256 had expired, 724 surrendered, 172 cancelled and 148 were invalid (Aaj TV report quoting BEOE). The high expiry and surrender numbers suggest closures as well as lapses. About 762,499 emigrants registered in 2025, so the case volume is concentrated in active OEPs.
result.reason: The duty is real and current under Pakistan's Emigration Ordinance and Rules 1979 (updated 2023). A licence lasts up to 3 calendar years. Renewal is on Form 3, filed at least a month before expiry, at Rs15,000 a year plus a late fee. Weak performance shortens the renewal to 1 or 2 years, and misconduct can mean refusal, suspension or loss of the security deposit. BEOE issues show-cause notices often. I found no commercial OEP back-office software. However, the per-worker steps (demand permission, emigrant registration, e-Protector) already run on BEOE's own OEP portal and permission system. So the leftover job is renewal reminders plus case files: infrequent and low value. I could not confirm any other recurring returns because both copies of the Rules failed to open. About 2,358 valid licences: a small market that pays little.

result.competitor: The core pilgrim-file workflow (contracting, visa submission, permits, pre-arrival data, transport orders) runs inside Saudi Arabia's mandatory Masar Nusuk / Nusuk business platform, which is free. I found no public API, so third-party tools can only sit beside it as a CRM or back office. On the Pakistan side, MoRA has a dedicated wing that verifies Umrah agreements and publishes the approved list itself. Generic or foreign tools exist: PHPTravels Umrah module, Umrah360 (it advertises 'Umrah Nusuk Information'), and the ECOSIRE Odoo Hajj/Umrah add-on (from USD 1,500). I found no Pakistan-specific compliance tool, but the compliance layer it would serve is thin.
result.duty: Partly confirmed. The Hajj and Umrah (Regulation) Act 2024 (Act XVII of 2024) is enacted: gazetted 30 Aug 2024 and in force at once. Its table of contents lists registration criteria, operator liability, complaint and appellate committees, blacklisting and a Penalty section. I could not read the operative text because the PDF pages are image-based. In July 2026 the Ministry of Religious Affairs (MoRA) issued a notification: only ministry-approved companies may serve Umrah pilgrims, operators must promptly verify their Nusuk agreements, and an approved list will be published. One report says the policy takes effect only after federal cabinet approval. Payment through banks and keeping receipts is advice to pilgrims, not an operator filing duty. I found no recurring return, register or reporting duty to MoRA. The Pakistan-side duty is effectively a yearly approval and agreement verification, and no concrete Pakistani penalty is stated beyond complaints and blacklisting. On the Saudi side, Ministry of Hajj and Umrah contract terms require agents to contract digitally through Masar Nusuk each season. They also require Saudi Umrah companies (and possibly agents) to enter pre-arrival data in the Nusuk business platform no more than 24 hours before arrival. That is the real operational workflow.
result.market: Small. An older MoRA figure, undated in the results, is about 600 companies registered for Umrah operations. The verified lists were 37 in Sep 2024, 53 in the first phase of Aug 2025, and 113 approved companies in Sep 2025. I found no 2026 count. Sub-agents and unregistered agents are more numerous but are not the ones carrying the duty.
result.reason: The regulation is real but the recurring Pakistani compliance task is thin. It amounts to yearly MoRA approval and verification of the Nusuk agreement, with no reporting or register duty found and no clear penalty beyond complaints and blacklisting. The day-to-day pilgrim-file work runs in Saudi Arabia's mandatory, free Masar Nusuk system, which publishes no API, so an MVP can't automate the core job. Verification is done by a MoRA wing, not the operators. The market is small: about 113 approved firms in 2025 and about 600 registered historically. Generic Umrah back-office tools (PHPTravels, Umrah360, the Odoo add-on) already cover the operations side. Pain is moderate and seasonal, and willingness to pay is unproven. I couldn't read the Act's penalty and registration sections.

result.competitor: I found no Pakistani AML/CDD software vendor for real estate DNFBPs. The only products found were UAE ones (amluae.com) and LSEG World-Check (enterprise, high price). Free state tools cover part of the job: the FBR DNFBP portal (registration and questionnaire), FMU goAML (STR/CTR filing), FBR's sanctions screening page, and simplified Urdu/English CDD forms. FBR also cut real estate reporting to four standards and sent teams to realtor associations. So the record-keeping and CDD file workflow is not automated by anyone, but the state's simplification lowers the pain.
result.duty: AML Act 2010 s.7A and the FBR AML/CFT Regulations for DNFBPs 2020 (SRO 924(I)/2020), with sanctions under SRO 950(I)/2020, require real estate agents to register with the FBR DNFBP Directorate. They must also do CDD on property purchases and sales, keep records, screen against targeted financial sanctions, answer the Offsite Monitoring Questionnaire, and file STRs/CTRs with FMU through goAML (the FBR portal links 'File STR or CTR with the FMU via GoAML'). S.R.O. 1439(I)/2026 of 27 Aug 2026 widened the definition to builders, developers, title-transferring authorities and brokers. It also added duties to keep records until litigation ends and to answer CDD requests from FBR, LEAs and FMU promptly. Since 1 Jan 2022, development authorities may not deal with unregistered agents. The plan to make builders' NOCs depend on DNFBP registration plus a compliance officer was reported on 29 May 2025 (Nukta), but I did not confirm it was formalized. FBR has fined and inspected agents. I did not find the specific amounts in SRO 950. The duty is per transaction (CDD) plus periodic (questionnaire, inspections).
result.market: About 22,000 real estate DNFBPs registered with FBR, out of an estimated 500,000 property dealers and developers (Dawn/IIPS/Graana; the figure is dated, from around 2021-22). SBCA alone oversees more than 5,000 builders and developers (Nukta, 2025). I found no current official count.
result.reason: The duty is real and was widened in Aug 2026 to builders and developers. No local software does the CDD file, record retention and goAML prep. Against that: small property dealers are largely informal and resist the rules, only about 22k of 500k are registered, and they are price-sensitive. FBR has deliberately simplified the forms and supports dealers through associations, and filing and registration are on free state portals. Builders and developers, if the NOC gating is enacted, are the better-paying segment (compliance officer, sanctions screening, record-keeping), but that gating is unconfirmed. Distribution through realtor associations is possible. A simple Urdu mobile CDD/record vault MVP is feasible, but willingness to pay and enforcement intensity are uncertain.

result.duty: Punjab Agricultural Income Tax Act 1997 as amended (2024/25), administered by the Board of Revenue Punjab. It requires an annual statement of agricultural income and landholding. Tax Year 2026 is the first year of online filing, with a deadline of 30 Sep 2026. PTBA asked for an extension to 31 Oct (pkrevenue). I found no official extension; Sindh's extension and the FBR extension to 15 Oct do not apply. Section 8 penalty for not filing: 0.1% of tax due per day or Rs1,000 per day, with minimums of Rs10k/20k/50k by income band (ict.edu.pk blog, a secondary source). Section 10 late-payment surcharge: the higher of 12% or KIBOR+3%. Uncertainty: the Punjab Assembly Speaker ruled the Board of Revenue rate notifications void on 20-21 Apr 2026 (reported via Dawn in the ICT blog; I did not verify this independently). The Finance Bill 2026 proposed higher per-acre rates; I did not confirm whether they were enacted.
result.market: About 396,000 Punjab taxpayers declared Rs293bn of agricultural income on federal returns for TY2025, out of about 445,000 nationally (ICT blog, a secondary source). result.reason: The duty is real. The Punjab AIT Act 1997 (amended 2024) requires an annual statement. The penalty for not filing is 0.1% of tax per day or Rs1,000 per day, with minimums of Rs10k, Rs20k or Rs50k depending on income. TY2026 is the first year of online filing. I found no extension notice. Filing runs through the Board of Revenue's free PITB app (registration, linked to PLRA and FBR) and its AIT Web Module (returns). I found no third-party software. That makes this an add-on to a free state portal. Some 396k Punjab taxpayers declared agricultural income on FBR returns, but about 95% of farmers fall under the threshold. The April 2026 Speaker ruling voiding the rate notifications adds legal uncertainty. Willingness to pay is low and rural buyers are hard to reach, so practitioners are the only realistic channel.

Enforcement is negligible (14,717 workers registered by 2021, per Pulitzer Center). The PESSI site and app already take registrations. Households number in the millions, but with no penalty enforcement the pain is low. I did not check the ICT Act or penalty amounts. Revisit only if Rules are notified.

Duty is real. Under the Punjab Food Authority Act 2011, every food business needs a licence valid for one year and renewed annually. Operating without one carries up to 1 year in jail or a Rs500,000 fine. A 2025-26 drive has inspected 62,000+ meat units, sealed 216 and fined Rs72.2m, and PFA says it will register all slaughterhouses. I found no third-party butcher compliance software. PFA has a free fee calculator and licensing portal (PITB), which covers the filing itself. The market is weak: butchers are informal, cash-based and low-margin, and the fee is set by business scale. Not checked: the number of butchers, any butcher-specific fee, and Sindh/KP equivalents. Willingness to pay is likely low, and the drive is enforcement-led.

The duty is real. The Punjab transport department FAQ says every public-service or goods vehicle needs a route permit and a fitness certificate, and goods-carrier permits run 3 years. I found no Pakistan-specific expiry-reminder product. Generic Odoo/ERPNext modules and the Pak Flexible GPS app exist, and e-Pay handles token tax lookup and payment. The claim's trigger is mis-framed. The 15 Oct 2026 Punjab PTA enforcement targets private cars (about 2.3M vehicles), not goods or bus fleets. Commercial vehicles already needed fitness certificates. The Sindh digitisation deadline and the penalty details were not verified. Buyers are fragmented, low-margin owner-operators who rely on agents, and I found no register count. Willingness to pay is weak.

The PM directive (late Jul/Aug 2026) to build an FBR-style fuel tracking system is real (Dawn, Business Recorder, Aaj). It is a directive to develop a system, not a rule on pump owners. No deadline, penalty, or pump-side filing is specified. OGRA already runs the Digital Sales Entry System at pumps, Rahguzar app, tanker tracking and depot telemetry. The state supplies these tools, so there is little room for a private compliance pack. Pump POS vendors (oscar.pk, e-invoicing.pk) already sell FBR POS. I found no official source that FBR POS is mandatory for pumps. About 12,000 pumps exist, a small market. The one concrete deadline is the SBP Raast QR mandate for pumps by 31 Jan 2027, from a search summary only. The different duty and buyer (Raast QR) was not verified. Score stays low.

The wheat permit regime is real. In July 2026 the Punjab Food Department suspended permits for Rawalpindi and Islamabad mills. In September 2026 mills announced a Punjab-wide strike over permits, with alleged bribe demands for permits. The department also runs the PITB-built Flour Ledger and a wheat permit portal. I found no private software competitor, but the state portal is the tool. I could not confirm the daily-entry duty, its penalty, or the legal basis in the sources I opened; the Foodstuffs (Control) Act citation is unchecked. Market size is unclear: only dated figures (204 mills involved in the 2020 crisis, 129 in Multan division) and nothing on chakkis. Rules are volatile, the problem is corruption and politics rather than software, and mills are unlikely to pay, so the score is low.

Duty is real: PFA SOPs (Nov 2025) require bottled/commercial water units in Punjab to change filters monthly, test monthly via PFA-approved labs, and upload filter-change video and lab reports to the PFA FBO Portal; non-compliant plants are sealed (deadline was 15 Dec 2025). No commercial compliance software found, but the state portal is the system of record and takes the uploads, so the added value is thin. Buyers are tiny, price-sensitive owners and enforcement is Punjab-only. Market count was not verified (Rawalpindi 246 plants is from the claim; 700 plants in the ProPakistani headline was not opened). Licence conditions and the portal's ease of use not verified. Low willingness to pay and a weak MVP wedge.

Duty is real. The Punjab Healthcare Commission (PHC) Act 2010 requires licensing of clinics, dental clinics and diagnostic centres. A regular licence needs full MSDS compliance, renews every 5 years after inspection, and failure to meet standards brings fines up to Rs 500,000 or closure. SHCC registration and licensing went online in June 2025 via SBOSS. I found no commercial readiness software, only official portals and PHC e-Certification training. But the duty recurs only every 5 years, enforcement is weak (Dawn: only 86 private facilities held a regular licence), and the claimed 23,041 figure is unverified. Sindh counts conflict: about 14,000 registered against 100,000 facilities. Willingness to pay is doubtful, and the idea overlaps K06 (waste and MSDS evidence for Punjab).
